--- title: "Item response models as neural networks" description: | The Rasch and 2PL models are tiny neural networks. Build them in PyTorch, widen the network, and ask whether it predicts held-out responses any better than the classical models, scored with the IMV on five IRW tables. format: html: code-fold: false toc: true toc-depth: 2 execute: echo: true eval: true message: false warning: false freeze: true --- A logistic item response model is a very small neural network. The Rasch model takes a person, looks up one number for them ($\theta_p$), takes an item, looks up one number for it ($b_i$), subtracts, and passes the difference through a sigmoid. In PyTorch terms that is two `nn.Embedding` layers and no hidden layer. The 2PL adds a second item lookup (the slope $a_i$). Once the models are written this way it is natural to ask what happens when the network is made wider or deeper: more latent dimensions, a nonlinear decoder. Does a neural network predict item responses better than the 2PL? This page builds the classical models in PyTorch, checks that they recover what the `mirt` package recovers, widens them, and scores every model on held-out responses from five IRW tables with the [InterModel Vigorish (IMV)](imv.qmd). Two more flexible one-dimensional models from R's `mirt` (the monotonic polynomial and an asymmetric item curve) are fit offline on the same split and join the comparison. ::: {#b6bc682d .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Setup"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import torch import irw from nn_irt_helpers import (TABLES, prepare, fit, predict, imv, log_loss, make_models, SEED) Rasch, TwoPL, Bilinear, MLP = make_models() torch.set_num_threads(4) plt.rcParams["figure.dpi"] = 110 ``` ::: ## The models, written as networks The four model classes below are the whole of the modelling code. Each takes a batch of person indices and item indices and returns a logit. | Model | Person lookup | Item lookup | Combine | |---|---|---|---| | Rasch | $\theta_p$ (1 number) | $b_i$ (1 number) | $\theta_p - b_i$ | | 2PL | $\theta_p$ (1) | $a_i, b_i$ (2) | $a_i(\theta_p - b_i)$ | | MIRT, $k$ dims | $\boldsymbol\theta_p$ ($k$) | $\mathbf a_i$ ($k$), $b_i$ | $\mathbf a_i \cdot \boldsymbol\theta_p - b_i$ | | MLP, $k$ dims | $\boldsymbol\theta_p$ ($k$) | $\mathbf v_i$ ($k$) | $\mathrm{MLP}([\boldsymbol\theta_p, \mathbf v_i])$ | The MIRT model is the compensatory multidimensional 2PL: $k$-dimensional person and item embeddings combined by a dot product, which is also a low-rank matrix factorisation of the logit matrix. With $k=1$ it is the 2PL; the page uses $k=2$. The MLP concatenates the two embeddings and passes them through hidden layers of ReLU units, so the interaction between person and item is no longer constrained to be a dot product. This is the shape used in neural collaborative filtering. Two sizes are fit, both on $k=2$ embeddings: a small one with a single hidden layer of 16 units, and a large one with two hidden layers of 64, so that depth is the only thing that changes. ::: {#8cf80c3d .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import inspect print(inspect.getsource(Rasch)) print(inspect.getsource(TwoPL)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` class Rasch(nn.Module): """logit P(correct) = theta_person - b_item.""" def __init__(self, n_persons, n_items): super().__init__() self.theta = nn.Embedding(n_persons, 1) self.b = nn.Embedding(n_items, 1) nn.init.normal_(self.theta.weight, std=0.1) nn.init.normal_(self.b.weight, std=0.1) def forward(self, p, i): return (self.theta(p) - self.b(i)).squeeze(-1) class TwoPL(nn.Module): """logit P(correct) = a_item * (theta_person - b_item).""" def __init__(self, n_persons, n_items): super().__init__() self.theta = nn.Embedding(n_persons, 1) self.b = nn.Embedding(n_items, 1) self.log_a = nn.Embedding(n_items, 1) nn.init.normal_(self.theta.weight, std=0.1) nn.init.normal_(self.b.weight, std=0.1) nn.init.zeros_(self.log_a.weight) def forward(self, p, i): a = torch.exp(self.log_a(i)) return (a * (self.theta(p) - self.b(i))).squeeze(-1) ``` ::: ::: The full source of all four, and of the training loop, is in [`nn_irt_helpers.py`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_helpers.py). ## Held-out cells, not held-out people Every one of these models has a parameter per person. A model cannot predict a person it has never seen, so the usual split by rows (train on some people, test on others) is impossible. Instead we hold out **cells**: 20% of each person's responses, chosen at random, are hidden during training and predicted afterwards. Every person and every item stays in the training set. The same mask is used by every model, including the `mirt` fits, which see the held-out cells as missing. The tables are all dense and dichotomous. They were chosen to vary in size and in how much structure beyond a single dimension there is to find. Tables with more than 5,000 respondents or 116 items are subsampled to those caps (fixed seed) so that every fit on the page stays small; the sizes below are the originals. | Table | What it is | Persons x items | |---|---|---| | `borges_brazil_residency_2024_cbt` | Brazilian medical residency entrance exam, computer-based form | 3,223 x 120 | | `encceja_2024_ef_lp` | Brazilian adult-education certification exam, Portuguese (INEP) | 23,462 x 30 | | `psychoneurotic_inventory` | Woodworth Psychoneurotic Inventory, yes/no symptom items | 6,019 x 116 | | `cdm_ecpe` | ECPE grammar test with a known three-attribute Q-matrix | 2,922 x 28 | | `art` | Author Recognition Test, native and non-native readers | 1,402 x 50 | ::: {#bb8b0b60 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} data = {t: prepare(t) for t in TABLES} pd.DataFrame({t: {"persons": int(d.pid.max() + 1), "items": int(d.iid.max() + 1), "train cells": int((~d.test).sum()), "test cells": int(d.test.sum()), "mean resp": round(float(d.resp.mean()), 3)} for t, d in data.items()}).T.astype({"persons": int, "items": int, "train cells": int, "test cells": int}) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: `prepare` calls `irw.fetch`, caches the table, subsamples, assigns integer indices, and draws the mask with a fixed seed. ## Rasch and 2PL in PyTorch Training is minibatch Adam on the binary cross-entropy of the training cells. One detail matters: fitting a free parameter per person by maximum likelihood is **joint** maximum likelihood, which is inconsistent as the number of persons grows and overfits persons with extreme scores. Adding an L2 penalty on the person embedding is the same as putting a normal prior on $\theta$, so the estimate is a MAP estimate and close to what `mirt` returns from marginal maximum likelihood. The `person_decay` argument sets that penalty. ::: {#ae5d0c76 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} d = data["borges_brazil_residency_2024_cbt"] n_p, n_i = d.pid.max() + 1, d.iid.max() + 1 rasch, h_rasch = fit(Rasch(n_p, n_i), d, epochs=30) twopl, h_2pl = fit(TwoPL(n_p, n_i), d, epochs=30) h_rasch.tail(1), h_2pl.tail(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` ( epoch train test 29 30 0.550568 0.559098, epoch train test 29 30 0.541612 0.549184) ``` ::: ::: Does the network recover the item parameters? Fit the same two models with the Python `mirt` package (marginal maximum likelihood on the training cells) and compare. ::: {#18895029 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} from mirt import fit_mirt wide = d[~d.test].pivot(index="pid", columns="iid", values="resp") wide_arr = wide.to_numpy(dtype=float).copy() wide_arr[np.isnan(wide_arr)] = -1 wide_arr = wide_arr.astype(int) m_rasch = fit_mirt(wide_arr, model="1PL") m_2pl = fit_mirt(wide_arr, model="2PL") fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4)) b_nn = rasch.b.weight.detach().numpy().ravel() b_nn = b_nn - b_nn.mean() ax[0].scatter(m_rasch.model.difficulty - m_rasch.model.difficulty.mean(), b_nn, s=12) ax[0].set(xlabel="mirt Rasch difficulty", ylabel="PyTorch Rasch difficulty") a_nn = np.exp(twopl.log_a.weight.detach().numpy().ravel()) ax[1].scatter(m_2pl.model.discrimination, a_nn, s=12) ax[1].set(xlabel="mirt 2PL discrimination", ylabel="PyTorch 2PL discrimination") for a in ax: lo, hi = a.get_xlim(); a.plot([lo, hi], [lo, hi], "k--", lw=0.8) plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](nn_irt_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){width=979 height=429} ::: ::: The gradient-descent fits land where the marginal-likelihood fits land. The Rasch difficulties are centred before plotting because the location of $\theta$ is not identified in the network (there is no prior mean), and the discriminations sit a little above the line because the person prior shrinks the $\theta$ estimates to a variance below one, and the slopes stretch to compensate; the ordering of items is the same. ## Widening the network Now the models that are not classical IRT. Train-versus-test log-loss by epoch makes the overfitting visible: once the test curve turns up, further training is memorising the training cells. ::: {#5ac3f1eb .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} curves = {} curves["Rasch"] = h_rasch curves["2PL"] = h_2pl _, curves["MIRT k=2"] = fit(Bilinear(n_p, n_i, 2), d, epochs=30) _, curves["MLP small"] = fit(MLP(n_p, n_i, 2, hidden=(16,)), d, epochs=30) _, curves["MLP large"] = fit(MLP(n_p, n_i, 2, hidden=(64, 64)), d, epochs=30) fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4), sharey=False) for name, h in curves.items(): ax[0].plot(h.epoch, h.train, label=name) ax[1].plot(h.epoch, h.test, label=name) ax[0].set(title="training log-loss", xlabel="epoch", ylabel="log-loss") ax[1].set(title="held-out log-loss", xlabel="epoch") ax[1].legend(fontsize=8) plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](nn_irt_files/figure-html/cell-7-output-1.png){width=979 height=429} ::: ::: ## Scoring with the IMV The IMV converts a log-loss improvement into a bet: if model 0 predicts held-out responses as well as a coin with bias $w_0$ and model 1 as well as a coin with bias $w_1$, the IMV is $(w_1 - w_0)/w_0$, the relative gain in the bettor's edge. The [IMV vignette](imv.qmd) has the definition and the R package; here it is in Python. ::: {#d931cdee .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(inspect.getsource(imv)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` def imv(y: np.ndarray, p0: np.ndarray, p1: np.ndarray) -> float: """InterModel Vigorish of model 1 over model 0 on held-out cells.""" w0 = equivalent_coin(log_loss(y, p0)) w1 = equivalent_coin(log_loss(y, p1)) return (w1 - w0) / w0 ``` ::: ::: Fit every model on every table. Each PyTorch model is trained for a fixed budget of epochs with the epoch of lowest held-out loss reported (early stopping, with the held-out set doing double duty as validation set; a production comparison would carve a third split). The `mirt` fits come from [`nn_irt_mirt_compute.R`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_mirt_compute.R), run offline on the same split. ::: {#294eac68 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Fit all PyTorch models on all tables"} from pathlib import Path def best_epoch_preds(model_fn, d, epochs=30): """Train, keep the predictions from the epoch with lowest held-out loss.""" te = d[d.test] best = (np.inf, None) model = model_fn() hist = [] for ep in range(epochs): model, h = fit(model, d, epochs=1, seed=SEED + ep) p = predict(model, te) ll = log_loss(te.resp.values, p) hist.append(ll) if ll < best[0]: best = (ll, p) return best[1] nn_specs = { "Rasch": lambda n_p, n_i: Rasch(n_p, n_i), "2PL": lambda n_p, n_i: TwoPL(n_p, n_i), "MIRT k=2": lambda n_p, n_i: Bilinear(n_p, n_i, 2), "MLP small": lambda n_p, n_i: MLP(n_p, n_i, 2, hidden=(16,)), "MLP large": lambda n_p, n_i: MLP(n_p, n_i, 2, hidden=(64, 64)), } preds = {} for t, d in data.items(): n_p, n_i = d.pid.max() + 1, d.iid.max() + 1 te = d[d.test] preds[t] = {"y": te.resp.values} for name, mk in nn_specs.items(): preds[t][name] = best_epoch_preds(lambda: mk(n_p, n_i), d) mp = Path("nn_irt_data") / f"{t}_mirt_preds.csv.gz" if mp.exists(): m = pd.read_csv(mp, dtype={"id": str, "item": str}) m = te[["id", "item"]].merge(m, on=["id", "item"], how="left") for c in m.columns: if c.startswith("mirt_"): preds[t][c] = m[c].values ``` ::: ::: {#f220f269 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="IMV chart"} rows = [] for t, pr in preds.items(): y = pr["y"] for name, p in pr.items(): if name in ("y", "2PL") or np.isnan(p).all(): continue rows.append({"table": t, "model": name, "log-loss": log_loss(y, p), "IMV vs 2PL": imv(y, pr["2PL"], p)}) res = pd.DataFrame(rows) order = [m for m in ["Rasch", "MIRT k=2", "MLP small", "MLP large", "mirt_2pl", "mirt_monopoly", "mirt_lpe"] if m in set(res.model)] labels = {"mirt_2pl": "mirt 2PL", "mirt_monopoly": "mirt monotonic poly.", "mirt_lpe": "mirt LPE"} colour = {m: ("#2a78d6" if not m.startswith("mirt_") else "#eb6834") for m in order} fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(TABLES), figsize=(11, 3.6), sharex=True, sharey=True) for ax, t in zip(axes, TABLES): sub = res[res.table == t].set_index("model").reindex(order) ypos = np.arange(len(order))[::-1] ax.barh(ypos, sub["IMV vs 2PL"], color=[colour[m] for m in order], height=0.65) ax.axvline(0, color="0.3", lw=0.8) ax.set_title(t.replace("_", " ").replace("borges brazil residency 2024 cbt", "residency exam") .replace("encceja 2024 ef lp", "ENCCEJA LP").replace("psychoneurotic inventory", "Woodworth"), fontsize=9) ax.set_yticks(ypos, [labels.get(m, m) for m in order], fontsize=8) ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=8) ax.grid(axis="x", color="0.9", lw=0.6); ax.set_axisbelow(True) for sp in ("top", "right"): ax.spines[sp].set_visible(False) axes[0].set_xlabel("IMV relative to PyTorch 2PL", fontsize=8, loc="left") from matplotlib.patches import Patch fig.legend(handles=[Patch(color="#2a78d6", label="PyTorch (MAP)"), Patch(color="#eb6834", label="R mirt (MML)")], loc="lower right", ncol=2, fontsize=8, frameon=False) plt.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.06, 1, 1)); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](nn_irt_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-1.png){width=1208 height=394} ::: ::: Bars to the right of zero mean the model predicts held-out responses better than the PyTorch 2PL on that table (which is the zero line, so it has no bar). The orange bars are R's `mirt` fit by marginal maximum likelihood on the same training cells, with each held-out cell predicted by its posterior-predictive probability (the item curve integrated over the person's posterior): the 2PL again, as the marginal-likelihood anchor for the PyTorch 2PL; the monotonic polynomial model, whose item curve is a flexible monotone function rather than a logistic; and the logistic positive exponent model (LPE), whose item curve is asymmetric. The last two change the *shape* of the item curve while keeping one latent dimension, which is the opposite move from the networks above. ::: {#be35d161 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="The numbers: IMV vs 2PL and held-out log-loss"} ll2 = pd.Series({t: log_loss(pr["y"], pr["2PL"]) for t, pr in preds.items()}, name="2PL") imv_tab = res.pivot(index="model", columns="table", values="IMV vs 2PL").reindex(order)[TABLES] ll_tab = res.pivot(index="model", columns="table", values="log-loss").reindex(order)[TABLES] ll_tab = pd.concat([ll2.to_frame().T, ll_tab]) pd.concat({"IMV vs 2PL": imv_tab.round(4), "held-out log-loss": ll_tab.round(4)}) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Three things stand out. **On the cognitive tests the 2PL is the model to beat, and nothing beats it.** On the residency exam, ENCCEJA and the ECPE grammar test every network is at or below the 2PL. The two-dimensional MIRT is the worst offender: with only 30 or 28 items per person its second dimension is fitted to noise, and early stopping cannot save it. The MLPs lose less, because their decoder is regularised by the same person prior and their extra capacity goes unused, but they do not gain. The ECPE result is the instructive one: the test has a known three-attribute structure, and a model built to find structure still does not predict better, because the attributes are so highly correlated that one dimension carries them. **Where the nets win, it is multidimensionality, and the MIRT finds it as well as the MLP.** On the Woodworth inventory, 116 yes/no symptom items spanning several syndromes, the two-dimensional MIRT beats the 2PL by about the same margin the 2PL beats Rasch. On the Author Recognition Test the gain is smaller and comes from a known second dimension, native versus non-native readers. In both cases the MLPs match or trail the MIRT: once the embeddings are two-dimensional, a nonlinear decoder adds nothing, and the large MLP is never better than the small one. Depth is not where the signal is. **Part of the apparent gain is estimation, not model.** The `mirt_2pl` row is the same 2PL as the PyTorch one and should sit at zero. It does not: marginal maximum likelihood with posterior-predictive held-out probabilities beats the MAP point estimates by a small margin on every table and by a noticeable one on the Woodworth, where persons have 116 responses and extreme score patterns. So the fair comparison for the networks is against the PyTorch 2PL (same estimator) and the fair comparison for the flexible item curves is against `mirt_2pl`. On that reading, the monotonic polynomial and the asymmetric LPE curve add almost nothing to the 2PL on any table (and the polynomial did not converge on the two 116-item tables), while the MIRT's gain on the Woodworth survives the estimation correction with roughly half its size. The page could close the estimator gap by integrating the networks' predictions over a person posterior too; that is a variational IRT, which is where the closing section points. ## What this page does not do The networks here see only person and item identities, exactly as the classical models do, so this is a comparison of functional forms, not of information. Models that use more information are a different question: sequential models of learning (knowledge tracing) use the order of responses; models with item text as input can predict items never seen in training; variational IRT replaces the point estimates with an encoder network that amortises person scoring. All of them can be scored with the same held-out cells and the same IMV. ## Further reading - Wu, Davis, Domingue, Piech & Goodman (2020), "Variational item response theory: fast, accurate, and expressive", *EDM*. - He, Liao, Zhang, Nie, Hu & Chua (2017), "Neural collaborative filtering", *WWW*. - Domingue, Kanopka, Stenhaug, et al. (2024), "The InterModel Vigorish as a lens for understanding and quantifying the value of item response models for dichotomously coded items", *Psychometrika*. - [IRT models in Python](irt_python.qmd), the companion page on `mirt` and `girth`. ## Reproducibility **Source code for this page:** [`nn_irt.qmd`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt.qmd), [`nn_irt_helpers.py`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_helpers.py) and [`nn_irt_mirt_compute.R`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_mirt_compute.R). This page is rendered with Quarto's `freeze` option: the PyTorch training runs on a laptop and the outputs are committed, so the site build does not need PyTorch. The five tables were fetched on 2026-10-15 from `item_response_warehouse` v72.0 (four tables) and `item_response_warehouse_6` v5.11 (`encceja_2024_ef_lp`), and are cached as `vignettes/nn_irt_data/*_split.csv.gz` together with the holdout mask. Seeds are fixed; versions below. ::: {#8e1c1d4d .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} import mirt, sys print("python", sys.version.split()[0], "| torch", torch.__version__, "| irw", irw.__version__, "| mirt", getattr(mirt, "__version__", "?")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` python 3.12.3 | torch 2.14.1+cpu | irw 0.7.4 | mirt 1.2.0 ``` ::: :::
